tagline.text: Seven waterfalls and a zipline canyon on the Lake Sebu highlands

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Lake Seloton, Lake Sebu, South Cotabato

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (entrance, zipline and transport, per person for a day trip)

children.text: Water from Lake Sebu flows past the Lonon River and Lake Seloton and then drops over seven tiers in this waterfall canyon. The headline attractions are the two-line zipline that starts at the first falls, the wide Hikong Alu and the tallest, Hikong Bente.

Seven Falls is a waterfall canyon in Barangay Lake Seloton, Lake Sebu, South Cotabato. Water flowing out of Lake Sebu follows the Lonon River into the small Lake Seloton, then tumbles down seven tiers of falls and continues to the Allah River. The lake area is considered an important watershed. Sitting on a plateau about
above sea level, the area is also cooler than the coastal lowland cities, which is part of its appeal.
The seven falls go by their T'boli names. The first, Hikong Alu, is about
(35 ft) tall and is the widest of the seven, while the second, Hikong Bente, is about

(70 ft) and is known as the tallest. The third to seventh are Hikong B'lebel, Hikong Lowig, Hikong Ukol, Hikong K'fo-i and Hikong Tonok, in that order. The first two are fairly easy to reach on foot, while the falls from the third onward are much easier to see from the zipline.
The zipline is what made this place famous. The long line that starts near the first falls is about
, and the return line is about
; the lines are described as crossing the canyon at roughly

above the ground at about 20 m per second. In a 2014 report the South Cotabato provincial government billed it as the highest and longest zipline in Southeast Asia and said the site drew about 300 visitors a day. Fees and operations have changed over the years, so check locally before you go.

The falls are on private land. One travel blogger wrote that the land is shared among 11 landowners and that the first five falls belong to the Dongon clan. Entrance and zipline fees are income for local residents, and it is much easier to get around if you ask the local people who guide you. Lake Sebu's lakeside town and T'boli cultural sites are close by, so the falls combine well into a single day. The lake covers about 354 hectares, reaches a maximum depth of about

, has 11 islands or islets, and was recognized as the ancestral domain of the T'boli and Ubo peoples by a 1993 DENR administrative order. Please remember that this is home to an Indigenous community and visit respectfully.
At about

, it is known as the tallest of the seven falls. One account says it takes less than five minutes to walk from the entrance gate to the base, so it is the easiest to get close to. On sunny days a rainbow often hangs in the spray.
About

tall, but the widest of the seven falls. A concrete bridge serves as a viewing deck, and the zipline start is right next to it. From the second falls you can take a motorcycle taxi or climb 774 steps.
The long line is about
and the return line about
. From about
above the ground you look down across the second through fifth falls. Many people ride for the scenery rather than the length.

Hikong B'lebel, Lowig, Ukol, K'fo-i and Tonok are hard to reach on foot and better seen from the zipline and the viewpoints. The viewpoint where the third, fourth and fifth falls appear side by side is the classic photo spot. You can walk the viewpoint section even if you do not ride the line.

Near where the second line ends there are T'boli traditional costumes for rent and souvenir shops. Many visitors take photos in the costumes, and you can also look at woven goods and brass crafts. Rental and sale prices differ by shop, so ask first.
The viewpoints over nearby Lake Lahit and Lake Sebu are scenic and make a good stop after the zipline. One trip report describes a short stop near Punta Isla Resort before heading back.
Leave General Santos or Koronadal (Marbel) for Lake Sebu. If you rely on public transport, start early in the morning so you do not miss the ride back.
Arrive in Lake Sebu town and take a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) to the Seven Falls entrance. In a 2013 account the one-way fare was about
Pay the entrance fee (
in past accounts), then walk down to the base of the second falls, Hikong Bente, for photos.
Go from the second falls to the first by motorcycle taxi, or climb the 774 steps, to reach the zipline start.
Ride the zipline across the second to fifth falls, then return on the return line.
Browse the T'boli costume rentals and souvenir shops, then head to a lake viewpoint.
Confirm the last ride back and head out. In a 2010 account the last jeepney from Lake Sebu to Surallah left around 4 PM, so be sure to check locally.
If you can spend a night in the lake town, a two-day trip with the falls on day one and the lake and cultural sites on day two is more relaxed.

items.title: Two-day route
items.subtitle: Falls and lake town at an easy pace

children.text: Leave General Santos and reach Lake Sebu before lunch to drop your bags at your lodging.
Enjoy the second falls and the zipline at Seven Falls, then visit the viewpoints.
Explore the lake area and T'boli cultural sites. See the Lake Sebu entry as well.
Return to General Santos. Shared vans toward Marbel run irregularly, so leave with time to spare.

Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific are reported to fly from Manila to General Santos International Airport (GES) every day. There are also flights from Cebu and Iloilo, so check the latest schedules.
From the airport, take a taxi or tricycle to Bulaong Terminal to start the overland leg.
From Davao, take a bus from Davao Ecoland Terminal to Marbel (Koronadal); it takes more than 4 hours. The fare was about ₱350 in 2017.

items.title: Bus and van from General Santos

children.text: A direct Yellow Bus Line (YBL) bus from Bulaong Terminal to Marbel takes about
1 hour
; the 2017 fare was about ₱100 (₱83 in a 2013 account).
From Marbel Terminal, take a van to Lake Sebu, which takes about
1.5 hours
. Service is irregular, so check locally.
The route via Surallah takes about
30 minutes
by bus to Surallah, then about
45 minutes
by jeepney from Surallah Terminal to Lake Sebu; the last trip is usually around 6 PM.
Most people take a motorcycle taxi from Lake Sebu town to Seven Falls. It cost about ₱50 in a 2013 account.
You can also use a rental car or a chartered vehicle; negotiate the fare locally and check the road conditions.

Seven Falls can be visited year-round. Right after heavy rain, however, the water rises, the canyon paths become slippery and the water can turn muddy, which hurts photos, and the zipline may stop depending on the weather.

Rainbows appear most often when the sun is out, and you will only enjoy the scenery from the zipline properly on a clear day. Fees are said to rise and crowds grow on weekends and holidays, so weekday mornings are more relaxed.

rows: Sunny, with rainbows over the falls
The best time for both the zipline and photos.
The flow is stronger, but take care on the canyon paths and check whether the zipline is running.
Visit on a weekday morning if possible.

Lodging ranges from lakeside resorts to lodges in town. A 2017 listing gave Sunrise Garden Lake Resort in Lake Seloton from ₱800 and El Galong Waterpark Resort in the poblacion from ₱900, and Punta Isla Resort and Lemobung Lodge and Restaurant are also known. Rates and operating status change, so confirm before you book.

The signature dish is grilled tilapia raised in the lake. Restaurants around the lake grill or fry fresh tilapia, and in the cool highland weather a hot soup also goes well. Check menus and opening hours locally.

If you plan a day trip by public transport, be sure to check the last ride out from Lake Sebu to Surallah. In a 2010 account it was around 4 PM, and a traveler who missed it had to hire a motorcycle taxi.
Weekday zipline fees are said to be lower than weekends and holidays, and there are fewer visitors.
Clear days give you a good chance of rainbows, so see the falls from below first and ride the zipline afterward.
The path down to the second falls is wet and slippery. Non-slip shoes are safer than flip-flops.
Keep your belongings in a waterproof bag. Some spots get heavy spray, and bring a strap so your phone does not fall from the zipline.
Local residents or the landowning family sometimes show visitors the way. A small tip is a polite way to say thanks.
When renting T'boli costumes or buying souvenirs, confirm the price first and negotiate politely. Ask local people for permission before photographing them.
Fees, hours and whether the zipline is running have changed over the years. The prices here mix accounts from 2010 to 2017, so always confirm locally before you go.
The zipline is an aerial ride, so check the safety gear and helmet yourself, and avoid it if you have heart or back problems.
Operations can stop on rainy or windy days.
Canyon paths and steps are damp and slippery. Children and older visitors should move slowly with a companion.
Check locally whether swimming below the falls is allowed and how deep it is, and watch for strong currents and swollen water.
The last public transport leaves early and van service is irregular. Leave plenty of time.
A highland lake town close to the falls. You can enjoy the lake and T'boli culture, and from town you reach the falls by motorcycle taxi.
A festival showing T'boli traditional culture, worth combining if the dates fit. Check the latest announcements for the schedule.
A volcanic lake in T'boli country that offers trekking. Check the latest announcements for access and safety information.
The gateway city with the airport and the bus terminal for Lake Sebu. Take a bus from Bulaong Terminal to Marbel.
